title: Why it’s so hard to predict a tragedy like Nepal’s glacier collapse - grist.org
description: Why it’s so hard to predict a tragedy like Nepal’s glacier collapse  grist.org
publisher.title: grist.org
full_article:
On August 26, the side of a mountain near the border between Nepal and Tibet collapsed. Seven billion cubic feet of glacial ice and rock, enough to fill 100 football stadiums, crashed roughly a mile straight down into the river below. The impact created a muddy wall of water that swept through the valley as fast as 100 miles per hour, destroying villages dozens of miles downstream and killing more than 1,300 people. Thousands more remain missing.

The scale of the disaster is extraordinary, even for a region accustomed to deadly floods and landslides. It will take months for scientists to confirm exactly what happened. But, they warn, one thing is already clear: As climate change melts icy landscapes worldwide, tragedies like this are more likely to happen. They are also incredibly hard to predict.

“Glacial loss destabilizes slopes in many far-reaching ways that are often unpredictable and catastrophic,” said Mark Carey, a professor of environmental studies and geography at the University of Oregon who leads a lab that studies glaciers. Proactive research and monitoring have saved lives in some parts of the world, Carey said, but in a place like the Himalayas, where thousands of glaciers are spread over vast areas, “it’s impossible to predict everything and establish early warning systems everywhere.”

The world’s glaciers have shrunk by about one-fifth in the last century and are expected to lose at least another quarter of their mass by 2100. Each fraction of a degree of warming makes them vanish faster, with hundreds of billions of tons of ice lost each year.

The downstream effects of this disappearing ice are complex and varied. Glaciers often buttress the sides of mountains and, as they retreat, newly exposed silt and rock can become unstable. The soil itself is also often glued together by a frozen layer known as permafrost, which helps lock slopes into place, but thaws when temperatures become too warm. Glacial meltwater can eat into the cracks in the bedrock, weakening it over time. All of these processes can result in sudden avalanches or rock slides — like one that caused a 1,500 foot tsunami in Alaska last summer, or possibly like the collapsed mountain slope in Nepal.

It’s also common for retreating glaciers to leave behind ridges of dirt and rock, known as moraines, that trap meltwater and rain. These natural dams can release enormous amounts of water if they break.

Glaciers themselves can behave as dams, too. In Juneau, Alaska, glacial meltwater has triggered flooding every year since 2011. Just north of the city, a glacier-dammed valley, known as Suicide Basin, fills with meltwater and rain throughout the year. When it becomes too full, the ice holding back the water lifts up, releasing billions of gallons at once. But while the yearly flood causes plenty of property damage, it has never killed anybody. That’s because it’s carefully monitored, said Eran Hood, a hydrologist and professor of environmental science at the University of Alaska who studies the basin.



“Every single cell phone in Juneau goes off when the lake starts to drain,” he said. “We have a lake in a known location, we have cameras all over it, we have a laser measuring the elevation of the water, and we have the ability to make drone maps every few weeks to update our estimates of the volume of water in the lake.”

Close monitoring and engineering has successfully prevented disaster in Peru as well. The country has spent decades draining dozens of high-risk glacial lakes across the Andes, “no doubt saving tens of thousands of lives,” said Carey, who wrote a book, In the Shadow of Melting Glaciers , about these measures. And last year, Swiss authorities were able to evacuate 300 residents from the Alpine village of Blatten just days before a glacier collapsed and engulfed it in an avalanche.

But success stories like these stand in stark contrast to what happened in Nepal, Hood said. While early-warning systems in the Himalayas monitor water levels in some high risk rivers and lakes, there is no regional system capable of continuously watching for the kind of sudden rock-and-ice collapse that triggered the disaster. Doing so would require intensive research and surveillance across a vast, remote, and difficult-to-access landscape where resources are limited.

“There’s really no effective way to monitor all these glaciers,” Hood said. “When you’re dealing with something that releases immediately and moves downslope so quickly, how can you find a way to provide people with any warning?”

The village of Blatten, Switzerland in May 2025 after a glacier collapse. Fabrice Coffrini / AFP via Getty Images

Emerging or repurposed technology may be able to help fill some of these gaps, said Dan McGrath, a glaciologist and associate professor at Colorado State University.

In places like Mexico City, seismic early-warning systems have sometimes given residents more than a minute to prepare before strong earthquake shaking arrives. Scientists are now wondering whether these same networks could be used to detect landslides and floods caused by glaciers. The glacial-break in Nepal caused readings equivalent to a 5.2 magnitude earthquake that traveled as far as Alaska, leading authorities to initially assume a seismic event had caused the disaster. There, too, just a few minutes of warning was shown to make all the difference. After warnings of the flood reached a school downstream, the principal was able to evacuate 900 students to safety before the torrent submerged it.

Researchers have also recently experimented with laying fiber-optic cables across a glacier in Switzerland to detect “icequakes,” or tiny fractures in the ice that generate seismic vibrations and could provide clues about changes in a glacier’s stability.

A new satellite, recently launched jointly by the United States’ and India’s space agencies, also holds promise. Known as NISAR, it was designed to detect subtle changes in Earth’s surface, like shifting glaciers, and can capture detailed information about ice and snow cover while seeing through cloud cover in ways that previous satellite sensors were not capable of. Recent analysis of the satellite’s data showed that it had recorded slumping on the mountain slope in Nepal several weeks before it collapsed.

But still, there’s no silver bullet, McGrath said. “Many of these mountain ranges are at a tipping point,” he said. “Freezing, or not freezing, is binary. And as temperatures warm above that and permafrost thaws, that is undoubtedly going to lead to an increase in disasters like this.”

title: MSF response not needed in Nepal following flash floods - MSF - Médecins Sans Frontières
description: MSF response not needed in Nepal following flash floods  MSF - Médecins Sans Frontières
publisher.title: MSF - Médecins Sans Frontières
full_article:
The human cost of the flash floods in Nepal of 26 August is devastating. Thousands of people have been killed, with many still missing, and many thousands more have lost their homes and livelihoods.



After arriving in Nepal on 27 August, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) teams have carried out assessments in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, the parts of Nepal worst affected by the flash floods. Our teams spoke with people affected, visited health facilities and relief centres, and spoke with municipal, district and disaster management authorities coordinating the response to this tragedy.



People have repeatedly told us that their biggest needs now are for recovery – for roads and markets to reopen, for schools, homes and infrastructure to be rebuilt. It is clear that continued, significant, relief efforts and funding for people in affected communities is required now and in the weeks and months to come.



As an emergency humanitarian medical organisation, MSF’s expertise is in providing humanitarian assistance in the most acute phases of emergencies. Our teams have assessed that the humanitarian response is well mobilised and managed. The government-led response, in coordination with local communities, United Nations agencies, and other humanitarian organisations, has succeeded in meeting people’s immediate humanitarian needs.



MSF has therefore decided not to launch a humanitarian response, as our expertise does not lie in the recovery, rehabilitation, and reconstruction activities that people in Nepal now need. We extend our admiration and respect to local communities, the Nepali authorities and all those responding tirelessly under difficult conditions, helping people recover from this disaster.



We send our heartfelt sympathies to the people of Nepal and all those who have lost loved ones in this tragedy.

title: Rescue teams in Nepal are digging for people missing after floods and mudslides, Al Jazeera English reports, with the same saturated, unstable ground that buried them now slowing crews sent to reach them - Space Daily
description: Rescue teams in Nepal are digging for people missing after floods and mudslides, Al Jazeera English reports, with the same saturated, unstable ground that buried them now slowing crews sent to reach them  Space Daily
publisher.title: Space Daily
full_article:
Rescue crews working in flood-hit areas of northern Nepal are still searching for people listed as missing nearly two weeks after catastrophic flooding swept through communities near the Nepal–China border. Al Jazeera English reported that operations had entered their 12th day, with geography, adverse weather and poor connectivity complicating work at flooded hydropower tunnels in Nepal. Across the border region, deep mud and the risk of further landslides have also slowed rescue work.

The accompanying Al Jazeera English report focuses on the difficult and dangerous conditions facing teams searching through the affected districts. Roads, tunnel entrances and recognizable landmarks have disappeared beneath debris, forcing crews to establish safe access before they can move equipment or begin digging.

A likely glacial collapse, then a search that narrowed to tunnels

The disaster struck on 26 August 2026. Authorities cited by Al Jazeera said the flooding was likely caused by a glacial collapse, while Reuters described a huge mass of mud and rock falling into a river after part of a glacier collapsed near the border between Nepal and Tibet. The resulting floods and mudslides swept through valley communities, buried roads and damaged hydropower infrastructure.

At hard-hit hydropower projects in Rasuwa and along the Trishuli corridor, attention soon turned to tunnels and underground facilities where workers might have taken shelter or become trapped. The Kathmandu Post, citing a Nepali Army briefing, reported that approximately 121 people could be trapped inside flood-hit hydropower tunnels. That figure represents part of a larger group of about 900 people who were initially reported unaccounted for at the affected projects. Officials stressed that the 900 figure did not mean all of those people were underground.

The same distinction appears in Reuters reporting carried by SRN News. Reuters also reported that four people had been rescued in recent days: two hydropower workers pulled from a tunnel on Friday, a Chinese national recovered from another tunnel on Saturday and a Nepali woman rescued from her buried house that same day. Officials said the tunnel searches would continue.

Why the ground itself sets the pace

Earlier field reporting from the Kathmandu Post described a tunnel entrance buried beneath thick slurry and surrounding terrain altered so extensively that rescuers could not initially locate the entrance. Project engineers had to use structural plans to identify its position before military engineers could break through the obstruction.

The Nepali Army’s later site-by-site briefing showed how the difficulties varied among projects. At Trishuli 3B, crews were clearing debris to make room for excavation equipment. At Chilime, teams were using a small excavator and a pump to remove sludge, while an excavator delivered by helicopter had to be moved toward the site with ropes. At Upper Trishuli-1, teams were searching with thermal-imaging cameras.

Destroyed roads and bridges have added another constraint. Equipment, fuel and personnel cannot move normally through the affected corridor, leaving helicopters and temporary access routes to carry much of the burden. Al Jazeera reported that adverse weather, difficult geography and limited connectivity continued to hinder operations at the tunnels, while landslide risks remained a concern across the border region.

The result is a cautious operation in which crews must first locate buried entrances, clear mud and debris, bring in suitable equipment and assess whether underground spaces can be entered safely. That combination helps explain why the search has continued for days even as teams remain under pressure to reach anyone who may still be alive.

Tallies that are still moving

As of Al Jazeera’s 6 September report, at least 1,384 people had been killed and more than 5,500 remained missing across Nepal and Tibet. Nepal’s national disaster agency reported that 1,341 bodies had been retrieved and approximately 4,996 people were still missing. Chinese authorities reported 43 deaths and 519 missing in Tibet.

Al Jazeera’s earlier 3 September account put the combined death toll at more than 1,280 and the missing count above 5,600. The difference illustrates how quickly official totals were changing as bodies were recovered and missing-person records were updated.

Those remain working totals rather than final figures. Missing-person lists can change as duplicate reports are removed, people are located safely and employers or authorities reconcile incomplete records. Search operations have continued, and officials have not declared the tunnel searches complete.

The United Nations and humanitarian partners have launched a $49.6 million flash appeal intended to assist more than 84,000 people. That support is arriving in a region where transport routes, power systems and water infrastructure have been badly damaged. For rescue crews, the immediate task remains unchanged: reaching places where the flood erased roads, buried entrances and left the landscape itself standing between them and the missing.

title: Nepal glacier saw exceptional heat before collapse caused deadly floods: researcher - Yahoo
description: Nepal glacier saw exceptional heat before collapse caused deadly floods: researcher  Yahoo

full_article:
The mountain section whose collapse triggered fatal floods in Nepal and China on August 26 had experienced unprecedented heat for the time of year, meteorological data analysed by a researcher shows.

Average temperatures on the mountain glacier at an altitude of 5,200 metres (17,060 feet) were estimated at around five degrees Celsius between August 21 and 26.

This is exceptionally high.

They had not exceeded 4.0C over the same period in more than 55 years of data recording, although no direct link to the collapse has so far been established.

This series of highly localised temperatures was reconstructed by Robert Rohde, chief scientist at the independent Berkeley Earth organisation in California.

At the site of the collapse, the average temperature recorded over that six-day period has risen by about 1.8C since the mid-20th century.

Without the additional heat brought by climate change, a comparable temperature pattern "would probably occur only once in a few thousand years", Rohde calculated for AFP.

The collapse came during the Langtang region's fourth-hottest summer on record, according to AFP's analysis of data from Europe's Copernicus observatory dating back to 1970.

- Tipping point -

"These hot conditions can also explain permafrost thaw and combined slope and glacier collapse," said French climatologist Valerie Masson-Delmotte.

Permafrost acts as ice cement, holding rock faces together. Its degradation makes them more unstable.

Satellite images also showed significant snowmelt in the days before the disaster, providing "a substantial source of liquid water that can infiltrate fractures in the mountain and facilitate landslides", said Etienne Berthier, a glaciologist at France's CNRS research agency.

Experts remain cautious, however, about the precise role played by the heatwave.

"It's not as straightforward as 'high temperature equals collapse,'" Kristen Cook, a geomorphologist at the Grenoble Alpes University in France, told AFP.

"If the temperature acted as a trigger, it seems that it needed to wait until the rock was right at the tipping point of collapse," she added.

Researchers are now examining the small movements observed in the mountain in the years before the collapse and their interaction with changes in temperature.

"Proving the rock near the fracture plane was significantly weakened as a result of meltwater and/or permafrost thaw" would be a "smoking gun" of climate change, according to Rodhe of Berkeley Earth.

full_article:
The committee, headed by Vice Chairman of Nepal’s National Planning Commission Gunakhar Bhatta, has six weeks to prepare a Post-Disaster Needs Assessment as a basis for mobilizing domestic and international resources for reconstruction.

Bhatta said the task force has begun collecting and analyzing data. The assessment is divided into 7 sectors – infrastructure, health, education, climate change, production, agriculture, and other.

Nepal has estimated property damage from the floods to be around 2.65 billion USD, affecting 7,570 houses and 33,000 people. The floods also damaged 48 government offices, 55 kilometers of roads, 37 vehicle bridges, 68 foot bridges, more than 1,800 hectares of agricultural land, and other infrastructure.

Nepal is continuing search and rescue and recovery operations. According to an official update on Monday, authorities have assisted 13,400 people in distress and recovered 1,385 bodies. Some 5,000 people remain missing, including roughly 600 foreign nationals from 35 countries.

title: Professor dies in Nepal flooding - The Duquesne Duke
description: Professor dies in Nepal flooding  The Duquesne Duke
publisher.title: The Duquesne Duke
full_article:
[Courtesy of Fevzi Akinci] Mark Cantrell, who taught at Duquesne, died on Aug. 26 in Nepal. He was 51.

Josh Imhof & Charlotte Shields-Rossi | news editor & a&e editor

When Urmi Ashar, assistant professor of Health Sciences at Duquesne, first met Mark Cantrell, the two immediately found common ground on one thing: their shared love of nature.

“One of the first things I had said when we had met was, ‘I’m happy to make the time for a meeting, but don’t get me seated in a room,’” Ashar said. “He smiled and said ‘We will get along great because I don’t like being indoors myself.’”

Cantrell died Aug. 26 in Nepal as a result of the deadly flooding and mudslides in the region, according to an email from Dean of the John G. Rangos, Sr. School of Health Sciences Fevzi Akinci.

Cantrell was returning to Nepal after going on a Yatra, a spiritual pilgrimage to Mt. Kailash in Tibet, China.

He was 51.

Born on February 25, 1975, Cantrell first came to Duquesne in 2021 when he was brought on to serve as director of public health for the university. He held the role for one year before stepping down to serve as a United States Diplomat with the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).

Still, he remained a part of the university as an adjunct professor until his death.

Laila Cronin, Duquesne public health alumna, met Cantrell while she was in high school in late 2021. When a family member found out that she was interested in studying public health, they helped her get in touch with Cantrell, who she said was happy to guide her.

Cronin, who was planning on applying to multiple universities, said that Cantrell was the reason she chose Duquesne.

“He was the only one that ever reached out about talking to me,” Cronin said.

Faina Linkov, associate Health Sciences professor at Duquesne, said this was not unusual for Cantrell.

“You really need to relate to students and make them feel like they belong … I heard from a couple of students that it was him that kind of solidified their decision to come to Duquesne,” Linkov said. “You don’t hear that often.”

Cronin had talked to very few professors before beginning college. She said she always thought of them as serious, but Cantrell wasn’t like that.

“He liked to crack a lot of jokes, [he was] very easy to approach,” she said. “He was so light-hearted about everything. It made it easy for him to joke about a lot of things and make you feel more comfortable.”

Although Cronin never had Cantrell as a professor, the two still kept in touch every now and then, calling and meeting in person. One time when the two were having a conversation, Cantrell brought up his plan to go to Peru.

“He is in his 50s and wants to live in another country for months. He must be very passionate,” she said she thought to herself.

Linkov said that she was always surprised at how engaged Cantrell could keep his students, especially when he was just starting out at Duquesne.

“I think for every person that I meet, there is typically a learning curve. It takes a while. It took me a year to settle in Duquesne,” she said. “For him, it was like he was always there.”

When he was there, Cantrell’s colleagues said he embraced all aspects of campus.

“We went up for lunch and then we just walked all through the different avenues in academic walk and the different avenues that you can because it’s a good workout, but we are also having a good conversation,” Ashar said. “That actually was the basis of our relationship.”

On these walks, she and Cantrell would often discuss the state of public health, how to better immerse students and what they could learn from smaller communities’ healthcare systems.

Cantrell would regularly travel the world with organizations like the World Health Organization and USAID, and would bring the knowledge he learned on those trips back to the classroom. He had a strong interest in teaching students about these systems, Linkov said.

“I think he had a very non-traditional sort of view about how to educate people, and so he was not thinking about traditional semesters,” Linkov said. “He was thinking more about kind of like short-term courses where you get exposed to local environments, local communities and you learn more.”

Ashar said this is why Cantrell joined USAID and also why it was so hard for him when the program was disbanded.

“I remember even at that time he had felt really upset, not about his job loss, but about the fact that we were leaving behind unfinished work and the communities that were dependent on us globally,” Ashar said.

Still, Cantrell did not let this sway him and remained a part of the public health community until his death, while continuing to look for new ways to advance the field. Ashar said this is what made him special.

“There are very few people I know, at least I have met, who can think about the big system that we are living in and it was a joy to get to know him,” she said. “Most people only focus on their jobs, their little part of the universe. He was different in that way.”

title: Nepali students share emotions about deathly flood - The Duquesne Duke
description: Nepali students share emotions about deathly flood  The Duquesne Duke
publisher.title: The Duquesne Duke
full_article:
[Courtesy of Bishnu KC] Nepali and Korean UNICEF works aid residents after flood in Nuwakot, Nepal.

Kaitlyn Hughes & Diva KC | editor-in-chief & layout editor

Although Dikaksha Dhital only spent three years of her life living in Nepal, the floods that hit the country Aug. 26 still hit close to home.

After seeing the country endure earthquakes and large-scale political protests, one thought came to Dhital’s mind — surprised, but not surprised.

“I think the shock factor came from how massive it was, how destructive it was and how many lives and houses it just took in a blink of an eye,” said Dhital, who is a senior health science major at Duquesne University.

The floods were caused by a glacial collapse near the border of Nepal and China that sent a flash flood and mudslide along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers, which has killed more than 1,300 people. This includes Mark Cantrell, who was a professor in the John G. Rangos, Sr. School of Health Sciences. He died in the floods and mudslides in Nepal at the age of 51.

The collapse of glacial rock and ice subsequently triggered a 5.2-magnitude tremor.

Nepal is located at the border of two large tectonic plates — the Indo-Australian and Asian plates — where collisions are frequent and lead to earthquakes, according to the University of Melbourne.

The country ranks 11th and 16th, respectively, in its vulnerability to earthquakes and combined disasters on the global scale, according to UNICEF.

“Growing up, I would hear about earthquakes and other natural disasters happening in Nepal so I just assumed it was one of those, not to diminish it … I didn’t realize how bad it was until I saw the one famous video where everything goes crashing down,” said Rakshya Kafle, a sophomore biochemistry major at Duquesne who is from Nepal.

The video Kafle is describing depicts gray mud and floodwaters shooting over a Chinese border patrol building on the border of Nepal and China. The building is then flattened by the fierce currents — along with many of those who were fleeing.

“Everytime we do make the news, it’s always something bad,” Kafle said.

Burdens of a small country

Kavya Odari, who is a junior in the business law program at Duquesne and from Nepal, said that the floods broke her heart.

“How much more can they even suffer through?” Odari asked.

There are 31.5 million people living in Nepal compared to the United States’ 342.6 million people, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.

“Nepal is a small country and not a lot of people know about it. … When I say I’m from Nepal, [people say] ‘Oh, where is that?’… In between China and India is what I’ve always said my entire life,” Kafle said.

Climbing temperatures lead to falling glaciers

The consensus among scientists is still open about exactly what happened to cause the amount of water that came with the flood, said Phillip Reeder, a professor in the department of civil and environmental engineering and sciences at Duquesne.

They know it has to do with glacier melting in the Himalayas, which Reeder said was caused by one thing: climate change.

“Between 1880 and now, the Earth on average has warmed 1.4 degrees centigrade [Celsius],” Reeder said. “That’s enough to knock all these Earth systems out of whack and to cause all kinds of cascading effects.”

With the Earth heating up, ice around the globe is going to start melting, Reeder said. Ice sheets are shrinking in Greenland, Antarctica and in high mountain areas, such as the Himalayas. Scientists are convinced this was the catalyst of the flood, Reeder said.

While climate change also affects the U.S., Odari said other countries feel it disproportionately, so getting educated on these topics is the least people can do.

“It’s like the first-world countries are creating these problems, and then consequently the third-world countries are bearing it,” Odari said.

The glacier that collapsed in the Himalayas was about a half mile wide.

“So you can imagine, that’s an enormous amount of ice,” he said.

But the question scientists are still trying to answer is: Where did all the water come from?

The flood in Nepal isn’t the only sign of climate change, Reeder said. The Earth is seeing more hurricanes, more active thunderstorms, more tornadoes and droughts.

“We’ve got to be really cognizant that we’re the stewards of the Earth here,” Reeder said. “Think about what can you do as an individual to help preserve the planet, and that doesn’t mean you have to go to Washington, [D.C.] to hold a sign and go to a rally or a protest or whatever. A lot of it is how you live your daily life.”

Knowing and helping Nepal

The worst part about the situation for Dhital and her cousin Ristha Kafley, who goes to the University of Pittsburgh, is being in the U.S.

“We can’t be there to actively help,” she said. “Being in the healthcare field, it definitely hits harder because it’s like if we were there, we’d be a part of the search and rescue team. We’d be there helping. We’d be there doing as much as we could in our power, and being here and not being able to do that, it’s just like okay. I just have to sit and trust my people that they have each other.”

The floods come at a time when people in Nepal are about to celebrate a significant religious celebration called Haritalika Teej on Sept. 13-16.

“This happening around the festival times is just really sad because we have people that are here celebrating the festival, but our people back home are suffering,” Kafley said.

Kafle said she wants people to be aware of the culture and people of Nepal, beyond the catastrophes the country faces.

There are about 3,203 Nepali people living in Pittsburgh’s metropolitan area, according to Neilsberg.

“The culture is right next to you,” Kafle said. “Not just knowing what happened but knowing Nepal and what it is beyond that.”

Diva KC can be reached at kcd@duq.edu

The death toll from Nepal's devastating flood rose on Tuesday to 1,357, with 5,326 people still missing, the country's disaster authority said nearly two weeks after the August 26 disaster.

In China, 43 people were confirmed dead and 519 missing, according to state media, bringing the overall toll to 1,400 dead and 5,845 missing.

Rescue work continued in Nepal for a 14th day after the devastating glacial and mountain collapse near the China-Nepal border swept away roads, bridges and homes.

Nepali rescuers are focusing on three hydropower projects where they believe workers could still be trapped, the disaster agency said.

Hundreds of hydropower workers are among the missing, but the rescue of three from deep inside tunnels -- two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday -- has raised hopes that others could still be alive.

"Our search and rescue operation is ongoing," Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of the country's disaster authority, told AFP.

"We are hoping that there might still be survivors in at least three projects, and we are pushing our operations there."

Foreign experts, including from China, India and South Korea, are aiding Nepali teams.

"We have also received reports that there are stranded people higher on the hill," Uprety added.

With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has buried hundreds of bodies in mass graves after collecting DNA samples for future identification, according to police.

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people that has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, has said reconstruction could cost billions of dollars.

David Fisher, of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, said reaching communities isolated by the floods was a daunting task because of "narrow and dangerous" access routes.

"Every delay means families wait longer for the support they urgently need," he said in a statement.

title: The families still searching after Nepal’s deadly flood - The New Arab
description: The families still searching after Nepal’s deadly flood  The New Arab
publisher.title: The New Arab
full_article:
Half-mast flags hung over Singha Durbar, the seat of Nepal's government, on Monday as the country observed the 13th day since the glacier collapse that sent floodwaters tearing down the Bhotekoshi River on August 26, killing more than 1,300 people.

For many Nepalese families, the 13th day carries particular significance in Hindu mourning practices, when rites are traditionally performed for the dead.

But with about 5,000 people still unaccounted for, including roughly 900 hydropower workers, 500 of whom are still believed to be trapped in tunnels, thousands of families are still waiting to learn of their loved ones' fates.

Kishan Adhikari, a civil engineer on the Upper Trishuli 3B project in Nuwakot, was conducting a routine inspection on the morning the flood hit. Then someone told him a flood was moving downstream.

Kishan called a senior officer at the project and asked him to check. The call lasted only moments. Between 9:22 and 9:24 that morning, the flood wave reached the site – just two minutes after he made the call and roughly seven minutes after an alert had been issued for his district.

A general view shows damaged houses covered in sludge in the aftermath of flash floods in Trishuli, in Nepal's Nuwakot district on September 6 [Getty]

"Until then, we had absolutely no information about the flood," Kishan tells ​​​​​​The New Arab . "I don't know what my mind thought or what decision I made, but I turned right. Maybe I survived because I turned right, but I couldn't save my other colleagues. I took off my boots and climbed straight up through the bushes."

From higher ground, he could see mudslides moving toward the project site and a handful of people who had escaped. The powerhouse, offices, staff quarters, and workers’ camp had disappeared beneath the floods.

"My daughter and mother were at the project quarters. I had brought them only a month earlier," he continues, breaking into tears. "I never thought something like this would happen."

To this day, neither his mother nor his daughter has been found, and Kishan has not left Kathmandu since.

He is still at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, where relatives of people who disappeared in Rasuwa and Nuwakot move between wards, lists, posters, and officials, looking for information.

People recover their belongings in the aftermath of flash floods at Devighat in Nepal's Nuwakot district on September 8 [Getty]

Names on a list

The Ministry of Health said on September 1 that only about 4 percent of the roughly 900 bodies recovered by then had been named.

One of the people still looking is Rakesh Prasad. He has spent several days at the hospital looking for his younger brother, Umesh Prasad, who was working as a builder at Sherpa Hydropower in Rasuwa. The brothers are from Motihari, across the border in India.

Umesh last spoke to his wife at about 7:30 on the morning of the flood. He has four children: girls aged 12 and 10, and boys aged 7 and 5.

"I only have a list forwarded to me by a relative with my brother's name on it," Rakesh tells The New Arab . "I have no idea who prepared the list, what it represents or whether being on it means my brother is missing or dead."

Hospital officials say there are no details of Umesh in their records.

Rakesh Kumar shows the random list he received which has the name of his missing brother, Umesh at list number 511 [Pratik Ghimire]

Sapana Sherpa, another concerned family member at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, travelled 260 kilometres from Khotang to Kathmandu in search of her uncle and his wife, who had lived in Rasuwa, where they ran a small hotel.

Her uncle, Dorchi Sherpa, had lived in Rasuwa for decades. Sapana had never met his wife, Sobita Tamang, and the family knew little about her. When she reached Rasuwa, villagers told her that her uncle and his children had been swept away. But there was still a possibility that Sobita had survived.

"We had never met her, so we contacted people in Rasuwa and asked them to send us photographs so we could identify her," she says.

"They said her name was also on a list, but nobody could tell us what kind of list it was."

At the hospital, however, her uncle’s wife's name did not appear on any of the official lists. With no other way to search for her, Sherpa pasted photographs of her uncle and aunt on the hospital walls.

"Thousands of photographs are pasted here by families looking for their loved ones," she adds. "I could only put up their photographs and hope that someone might recognise them or tell us what happened."

Sapana Tamang shows the photos of her missing uncle and aunt [Pratik Ghimire]

The trauma that follows

Four days after the flood, Aalok Mishra, a medical officer, travelled from Methinkot Hospital in Kavre to a temporary holding centre at Devighat in Nuwakot, one of several set up in the area.

The centre, operating from the Ayurvedic and Alternative Hospital, was treating 200 to 300 patients a day. Most had cuts, bruises and what appeared to be simple fractures. Others had suffered severe limb injuries or amputations. Those patients were stabilised at the centre before being taken by ambulance to Kathmandu, says Aalok.

"Wherever roads remained accessible to vehicles, the facilities were adequate," Aalok tells The New Arab. "From food and drinking water to medicines, the necessary supplies were available."

But across the Trishuli River from the centre, there were no roads. Supplies and patients on that side had to be moved by drone or helicopter, in operations jointly run by the Armed Police Force, the army and Nepal Police.

Patients were brought to Devighat for treatment and referred to Kathmandu if they needed care beyond what the centre could provide.

Medical teams rotated every three or four days. Aalok's team of four stayed for three days before another team took over, while an Armed Police Force medical team had been there since day one.

For Aalok, however, the flood's most difficult injuries were not always physical.

"Facing something we already know is one thing, but facing something sudden and shocking, which takes away a lifetime's earnings, the house and the entire family in a single moment, carried away by that flood," he shares.

He saw patients slip into depressive states, lose their appetites and withdraw from others, spending much of the day in profound sadness. His team and the Armed Police Force medical team provided counselling, while separate psychiatry teams rotated between the holding centres.

Security forces standby at a helipad in the permises of a hospital [Pratik Ghimire]

No early-warning systems

There was no early warning system when the glacier fell, according to glaciologist Rijan Bhakta Kayastha of Kathmandu University's Himalayan Cryosphere, Climate and Disaster Research Centre.

The terrain is extremely steep and uninhabited on both the Nepali and Chinese sides, with no trekking routes or trails, which is why the government did not install any systems there, Rijan tells The New Arab.

He estimated that the danger of further flooding has not completely subsided, as temporary ponds and lakes have formed in the affected area, raising the risk of sudden releases, debris flows, and secondary flooding. One of the ponds that has since formed at the collapse site. It has already burst twice.

"Nepal needs stronger monitoring and early-warning systems across its glaciated river basins, including round-the-clock monitoring during the monsoon," he explains.

Photos of the missing have been pasted by family members outside the hospital walls in the hope of any kind of identification and information [Pratik Ghimire]

The expert says the safest option would be to monitor Nepal's glaciated river basins from east to west, with personnel deployed around the clock during the monsoon months from June to September.

"The government has begun doing this, and the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology now has a camera-equipped system in place at the site," he adds.

But downstream, Nepal's existing flood-warning system did work. According to an NDRRMA report, the ice-rock avalanche struck at around 8:40 a.m., and the Bhotekoshi-Syafrubesi monitoring station stopped transmitting shortly afterwards.

By about 9:15 a.m., the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology had confirmed a major flood wave and issued warnings downstream.

NDRRMA said about 679,295 SMS alerts were sent. In Bidur, Nuwakot, the warning arrived early enough to help about 900 students escape uphill. But for some, the window was far narrower.

Kush Kumar Shrestha thought it was an ordinary flood. He walked toward the river to see what was happening, as his mother and others called after him: "The flood is coming. Don’t go over there!"

He heard a roar and then saw a section of the jungle-covered hillside give way, sweeping away the people standing on it.

"A sister was crying out, pull me, pull me, but I couldn't pull her, and when I looked back, she was gone," Kush tells The New Arab.

His uncle, just a step behind him, was swept away; his mother and sisters too. He is at the hospital now, looking for any news on any of his family members.

"I can't sleep, I can't eat, and whenever I close my eyes, that massive flood flashes right back," he shares.

He is at the hospital, still searching for any information about his family members.

Like other families, he has added their photographs to the walls, hoping that someone will recognise them or provide news of what happened.

The search has become increasingly difficult as the recovery of bodies has far outpaced their identification.

Meanwhile, the search for those still missing continues at 12 hydropower sites along the corridor, where the army and other rescue teams are digging through mud and debris in tunnels and damaged facilities.

Pratik Ghimire is a journalist based in Kathmandu, Nepal

title: Nepal-China flood death toll climbs to 1,400 - TRT World
description: Nepal-China flood death toll climbs to 1,400  TRT World
publisher.title: TRT World
full_article:
The death toll from devastating floods and mudslides along the Nepal-China border has risen to 1,400, with more than 5,800 people still missing, official figures showed on Tuesday.

Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 1,357 bodies had been recovered from flood-hit districts, while 5,326 people remained missing, including 587 foreigners.

More than 13,500 people have been rescued so far, with rescue operations continuing into the weekend.

Related TRT World - Nepal-China border floods death toll climbs to 1,385 as thousands remain missing

China reports additional deaths and missing

Across the border in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet, massive mudslides have killed 43 people, while another 519 remain missing, according to Chinese authorities.

The disaster has affected communities on both sides of the mountainous border, leaving thousands unaccounted for and prompting continued emergency operations.
